summary: This RFC describes layering CMP over HTTP and includes the RFC 9480 updates introducing CMP URIs with a well-known prefix. It obsoletes RFC 6712 and, together with RFC 9810, obsoletes RFC 9480.

plainLanguage.summary: CMP is the protocol a device uses to ask a certificate authority for a certificate, and to receive certificates and revocation information. This document says how to carry those messages over ordinary HTTP requests, so that they pass through the same proxies and firewalls as web traffic.

subtitle: How to carry Certificate Management Protocol messages in HTTP POST requests, at a well-known URL.

tldr.problem: The Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) needs a transfer mechanism so that end entities, registration authorities and certification authorities can pass PKIMessage structures to each other with connection and error handling.
tldr.mechanism: Each DER-encoded PKIMessage is sent as the content of an HTTP POST request with media type application/pkixcmp, and the CMP reply comes back in the HTTP response. Servers support the path prefix /.well-known/cmp.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 6712 and folds in the well-known URI changes introduced by RFC 9480. The requirement to support HTTP/1.0 is dropped.

today: RFC 9811 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2025. It obsoletes RFC 6712 and folds in the URI changes introduced by RFC 9480, and no later RFC is listed as replacing or updating it.

sections.title: Why CMP Needs a Transfer Protocol
sections.content:
The Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) requires a well-defined transfer mechanism to enable End Entities, Registration Authorities and Certification Authorities to pass PKIMessage structures between them.

The first version of the CMP specification included a brief description of a simple transfer protocol layer on top of TCP. Its features were simple transfer-level error handling and a mechanism to poll for outstanding PKI messages. It was also mentioned that PKI messages could be conveyed using file, email and HTTP based transfer, but those were not specified in detail.

Since the second version of the CMP specification incorporated its own polling mechanism, the need for a transfer protocol providing this functionality vanished. The remaining features CMP requires from its transfer protocols are connection and error handling.

CMP can benefit from using a reliable transport, because it requires connection and error handling from the transfer protocol, and HTTP covers all of these features. Additionally, delayed delivery of CMP response messages may be handled at transfer level, regardless of the message contents. Because RFC 9480 extends the polling mechanism of the second version of CMP to cover all types of PKI management transactions, delays detected at application level may also be handled within CMP, using pollReq and pollRep messages.

The usage of HTTP for transferring CMP messages exclusively uses the POST method for requests, effectively tunnelling CMP over HTTP. While this is generally considered bad practice, as set out in RFC 9205 for best current practice on building protocols with HTTP, and should not be emulated, there are good reasons to do so for transferring CMP.

HTTP is used because it is generally easy to implement, and it is able to traverse network borders using ubiquitous proxies. Most importantly, HTTP is already commonly used in existing CMP implementations. Other HTTP request methods, such as GET, are not used, because PKI management operations can only be triggered using CMP's PKI messages, which need to be transferred using a POST request.

With its status codes, HTTP provides the needed error reporting capabilities. General problems on the server side, as well as those directly caused by the respective request, can be reported to the client.

As CMP implements a transaction identification, the transactionID, identifying transactions that span more than just a single request and response pair, the statelessness of HTTP is not blocking its usage as the transfer protocol for CMP messages.
sections.plainLanguage:
CMP needs a way to move its messages around. The polling part was later built into CMP itself, so all the transfer protocol has to provide is a reliable connection and a way to report errors.

Wrapping a protocol inside HTTP is normally discouraged, but here it is practical: HTTP already crosses firewalls and proxies, and CMP software already speaks it. Only POST is used, because a certificate request has to be sent as a body, not asked for with a GET.

sections.title: The Form of a CMP Request
sections.content:
A DER-encoded PKIMessage MUST be sent as the content of an HTTP POST request. If this HTTP request is successful, the server returns the CMP response in the content of the HTTP response. The HTTP response status code in this case MUST be 200 (OK); other Successful 2xx status codes MUST NOT be used for this purpose. HTTP responses to pushed CMP announcement messages use the status codes 201 and 202 to identify whether the received information was processed.

While Redirection 3xx status codes MAY be supported by implementations, clients should only be enabled to automatically follow them after careful consideration of possible security implications, because the 301 (Moved Permanently) status code could be misused for permanent denial of service.

All applicable Client Error 4xx or Server Error 5xx status codes MAY be used to inform the client about errors. Whenever a client receives an HTTP response with a status code in the 2xx, 4xx or 5xx ranges, it MUST support handling response message content containing a CMP response PKIMessage.

The Internet media type application/pkixcmp MUST be set in the HTTP Content-Type header field when conveying a PKIMessage.
sections.plainLanguage: One request carries one certificate message, and one reply carries the answer. The reply uses status 200, and the body of the message is marked with the media type application/pkixcmp. Even an error status may still carry a certificate message in the body, so the client has to look at the content as well as the status.

sections.title: Where the Request Goes
sections.content:
Each CMP server on a PKI management entity supporting HTTP or HTTPS transfer MUST support the use of the path prefix /.well-known/ and the registered name cmp, to ease interworking in a multi-vendor environment.

CMP clients have to be configured with sufficient information to form the CMP server URI. This is at least the authority portion of the URI, for example www.example.com:80, or the full operation path segment of the PKI management entity. Additionally, path segments MAY be added after the registered application name as part of the full operation path, to provide further distinction. The path segment p followed by an arbitrary label could, for example, support the differentiation of specific CAs or certificate profiles. Further path segments, as specified in the Lightweight CMP Profile, could indicate PKI management operations using an operation label. The document lists four examples of valid full CMP URIs, from the plain well-known path to the path with both a name and an operation label.
sections.plainLanguage: The address of the service follows a fixed pattern, so that any client can find it without being configured with a special path: the request goes to /.well-known/cmp, with optional extra segments to pick out a particular authority or operation.

sections.title: Pushing Announcements
sections.content:
A CMP server may create event-triggered announcements or generate them on a regular basis. It MAY use HTTP transfer to convey them to a suitable recipient. In this use case, the CMP server acts as an HTTP client, and the recipient needs to use an HTTP server. As no request messages are specified for those announcements, they can only be pushed to the recipient.

If an end entity wants to poll for a potential CA Key Update Announcement or the current Certificate Revocation List, a PKI Information Request using a general message can be used instead.

When pushing announcement messages, PKIMessage structures MUST be sent as the content of an HTTP POST request. Suitable recipients might, for example, be repositories storing the announced information, such as directory services, which listen for incoming messages using the same HTTP Request-URI scheme.

The document lists the types of PKIMessage that are announcements which may be pushed by a CA, with the prefixed numbers reflecting the ASN.1 tags of the PKIBody structure: CA Key Update Announcement, Certificate Announcement, Revocation Announcement and CRL Announcement.

CMP announcement messages do not require any CMP response. However, the recipient MUST acknowledge receipt with an HTTP response having an appropriate status code and empty content, and when not receiving such a response it MUST be assumed that the delivery was not successful. If applicable, the sending side MAY try sending the announcement again after waiting for an appropriate time span. If the announced issue was successfully stored in a database, or was already present, the answer MUST be an HTTP response with a 201 (Created) status code and empty content. If the announced information was only accepted for further processing, the status code of the returned HTTP response MAY also be 202 (Accepted), after which the sender may try again after a delay and repeat this until it receives a confirmation that the announcement has been processed. A receiver MUST answer with a suitable 4xx or 5xx error code when a problem occurs.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate authority can also push news to a repository, such as a directory service, without being asked. The repository does not answer with a certificate message; it answers with an HTTP status only, and the sender keeps trying until it gets one that says the announcement was stored.

sections.title: Workflow and Implementation Notes
sections.content:
In CMP, most communication is initiated by the end entities, where every CMP request triggers a CMP response message from the CA or RA. The CMP announcement messages are an exception: their creation may be triggered by certain events or done on a regular basis by a CA, and the recipient of the announcement replies only with an HTTP status code acknowledging the receipt or indicating an error, but not with a CMP response.

If the receipt of an HTTP request is not confirmed by receiving an HTTP response, it MUST be assumed that the transferred CMP message was not successfully delivered to its destination.

Implementers should be aware that other implementations might exist that use a different approach for transferring CMP over HTTP. Further, implementations based on earlier documents that led to RFC 6712 might use an unregistered application/pkixcmp-poll media type, and conforming implementations MAY handle this type like application/pkixcmp.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the requester sends a certificate request and gets a certificate back. If no reply at all arrives, the request must be treated as not delivered. Older software may label its messages differently, so a server can be asked to accept that label too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All security considerations in HTTP apply, and the document adds five items for implementers and users to consider.

  • There is the risk for denial-of-service attacks through resource consumption by opening many connections to an HTTP server. Idle connections should therefore be terminated after an appropriate timeout, which may also depend on the available free resources.
  • Without being encapsulated in effective security protocols such as TLS, or without using HTTP digest, there is no integrity protection at the HTTP level. Therefore, information from the HTTP should not be used to change the state of the transaction, regardless of whether any mechanism was used to ensure the authenticity or integrity of HTTP messages.
  • Client users should be aware that storing the target location of an HTTP response with the 301 (Moved Permanently) status code could be exploited by a meddler-in-the-middle attacker trying to block them permanently from contacting the correct server.
  • If no measures to authenticate and protect the HTTP responses to pushed announcement messages are in place, their information regarding the announcement's processing state may not be trusted. In that case, the overall design of the PKI system must not depend on the announcements being reliably received and processed by their destination.
  • CMP provides inbuilt integrity protection and authentication. The information communicated unencrypted in CMP messages does not contain sensitive information endangering the security of the PKI when intercepted. However, it might be possible for an eavesdropper to use the available information to gather confidential personal, technical or business-critical information. The protection of the confidentiality of CMP messages, together with an initial authentication of the RA or CA before the first CMP message is transmitted, ensures the privacy of the end entity requesting certificates. Users of the HTTP transfer for CMP messages should therefore consider using HTTP over TLS or using virtual private networks, for example by utilizing IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: Five points matter. Too many open connections can exhaust the server, so idle ones should be closed. The HTTP layer itself has no integrity protection unless TLS or a digest is used, so an HTTP status alone must never change the state of a certificate transaction. A redirect can be used to block a client permanently. And a system must not depend on pushed announcements being received.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA made four updates. The reference for application/pkixcmp in the Media Types registry now points to this document instead of RFC 2510. The reference for application/pkixcmp in the CoAP Content-Formats registry points to this document instead of RFC 4210. The reference for cmp in the Well-Known URIs registry points to this document instead of RFC 4210. And the reference for p in the CMP Well-Known URI Path Segments registry points to this document instead of RFC 9480. No further action by IANA is necessary for this document or any anticipated updates.
sections.plainLanguage: The registries that list the media type and the well-known address were pointed at this document, so that anyone looking up the name finds the current specification.

viz.caption: CMP MESSAGES CARRIED IN HTTP POST REQUESTS (ILLUSTRATIVE)

messages.label: POST
messages.note: A DER-encoded PKIMessage in the body, with Content-Type application/pkixcmp.

messages.label: 200 OK
messages.note: The CMP response PKIMessage is in the body of the HTTP response.

messages.label: POST
messages.note: A pushed announcement, such as a CRL Announcement, with no CMP response expected.

messages.label: 201 Created
messages.note: Empty body: the announcement was stored.

viz.caption: THE HTTP STATUS CODES THIS DOCUMENT USES

items.label: OK
items.desc: The CMP response PKIMessage is in the body of the response.

items.label: Created
items.desc: A pushed announcement was stored in a database, or was already present.

items.label: Accepted
items.desc: A pushed announcement was only accepted for further processing.

items.label: Redirection
items.desc: May be supported, but clients should follow it only after considering the security implications.

items.label: Errors
items.desc: May be used to report errors, and the body may still carry a CMP response PKIMessage.

viz.caption: EXAMPLES OF VALID CMP URIS (RFC 9811 SECTION 3.4)
THE FIVE POINTS OF THE SECURITY SECTION

items.title: Idle connections
items.text: Terminate them after a timeout, so that many open connections cannot exhaust the server.

items.title: No integrity at the HTTP level
items.text: Without TLS or an HTTP digest, the HTTP layer must not be used to change the state of a transaction.

items.title: 301 Moved Permanently
items.text: A stored redirect target could be used to block a client from its server for good.

items.title: Pushed announcements
items.text: The design of the PKI system must not depend on announcements being received and processed.

items.title: Confidentiality
items.text: CMP messages are authenticated but not encrypted, so TLS or IPsec protects the requester's privacy.
